backstory.summary: Dr. Brian Foster, a physician in San Diego, consults attorney Lara Washington after being subpoenaed as a witness in a malpractice lawsuit involving a colleague. Lara counsels Brian on legal expectations, the scope of testimony, the attorney-client privilege boundaries, protecting his own interests, and dealing with professional anxieties ahead of the deposition. The conversation is a mix of practical logistics, legal guidance, professional sensitivities, and document handling.

conversation_transcript.speaker: User A
conversation_transcript.text: Hi Lara. I just walked in here. Thanks for making time to meet.

conversation_transcript.speaker: User B
conversation_transcript.text: Of course, Brian. Are you at your office or somewhere quieter?

conversation_transcript.speaker: User A
conversation_transcript.text: I’m in my office now. Closed the door so we can talk freely.

conversation_transcript.speaker: User B
conversation_transcript.text: Good. So, I reviewed the documents you sent. The subpoena requires you to appear at that building downtown next Friday at 10am.

conversation_transcript.speaker: User A
conversation_transcript.text: Okay, I saw the time but wasn’t fully sure which building.

conversation_transcript.speaker: User B
conversation_transcript.text: The San Diego County Hall of Justice. The address is on the first page.

conversation_transcript.speaker: User A
conversation_transcript.text: Got it. I think I know the place.

conversation_transcript.speaker: User B
conversation_transcript.text: You’ll be in Room 305 with Counsel for both sides and the court reporter.

conversation_transcript.speaker: User A
conversation_transcript.text: Who’ll be there from the hospital? Is Dr. Waters attending?

conversation_transcript.speaker: User B
conversation_transcript.text: I believe him, his counsel, and perhaps the coordinator for legal affairs. Not administration.

conversation_transcript.speaker: User A
conversation_transcript.text: That guy from legal, the one who sent me that memo—will he be present?

conversation_transcript.speaker: User B
conversation_transcript.text: If you mean Mr. Arnold, possibly. I’ll confirm with their office.

conversation_transcript.speaker: User A
conversation_transcript.text: Okay. I’m just worried about being alone on that side of the table.

conversation_transcript.speaker: User B
conversation_transcript.text: You won’t be. I’ll be sitting beside you the entire time.

conversation_transcript.speaker: User A
conversation_transcript.text: Thanks, that helps a lot. What should I bring with me there?

conversation_transcript.speaker: User B
conversation_transcript.text: Nothing except your ID and perhaps your calendar in case they ask about your recollections for that afternoon.

conversation_transcript.speaker: User A
conversation_transcript.text: Should I reference my phone or just memory when they ask about times?

conversation_transcript.speaker: User B
conversation_transcript.text: You can check your calendar if you need to be precise.

conversation_transcript.speaker: User A
conversation_transcript.text: Alright, I’ll bring the phone, and my badge. About privileged info—what counts in this setting?

conversation_transcript.speaker: User B
conversation_transcript.text: Don’t share any communications we have, or anything you learned exclusively from me. Stick to what you witnessed or did yourself.

conversation_transcript.speaker: User A
conversation_transcript.text: Understood. If they ask about those emails I got from admin, can I mention them?

conversation_transcript.speaker: User B
conversation_transcript.text: You can say you received hospital communications, but don’t disclose internal deliberations or confidential peer review content.

conversation_transcript.speaker: User A
conversation_transcript.text: What if they push me for more?

conversation_transcript.speaker: User B
conversation_transcript.text: Pause and look to me. I’ll object if the question is improper.

conversation_transcript.speaker: User A
conversation_transcript.text: Okay. Is there a difference between what I can say now and what I can say during the actual court case?

conversation_transcript.speaker: User B
conversation_transcript.text: Slightly. Depositions are broader in scope, but privilege still applies.

conversation_transcript.speaker: User A
conversation_transcript.text: So, about that patient—Mr. Hall—am I allowed to talk about any details?

conversation_transcript.speaker: User B
conversation_transcript.text: Only to the extent the subpoena covers facts you directly observed or actions you took. Avoid speculation.

conversation_transcript.speaker: User A
conversation_transcript.text: Understood. Should I review any other documents before then?

conversation_transcript.speaker: User B
conversation_transcript.text: Yes, briefly review your progress notes from that date and the consult note you sent to their team.

conversation_transcript.speaker: User A
conversation_transcript.text: I have those in my EMR here. Should I print them out, or is it fine to mention that I reviewed them electronically?

conversation_transcript.speaker: User B
conversation_transcript.text: You can refer to reviewing them electronically. No need to bring printouts.

conversation_transcript.speaker: User A
conversation_transcript.text: If they ask about the chart, do I need to describe everything, or just the relevant sections?

conversation_transcript.speaker: User B
conversation_transcript.text: Only the parts you personally entered or directly reviewed. Clarify if you didn’t author a section.

conversation_transcript.speaker: User A
conversation_transcript.text: If I’m unsure about timing, should I just say so?

conversation_transcript.speaker: User B
conversation_transcript.text: Absolutely. Be clear about what you recall, and don’t guess.

conversation_transcript.speaker: User A
conversation_transcript.text: I might have to reschedule that clinic later that day, depending on how long this goes.

conversation_transcript.speaker: User B
conversation_transcript.text: That’s wise. I estimate you’ll be out of there by noon, but set expectations with your staff just in case.

conversation_transcript.speaker: User A
conversation_transcript.text: Should I tell Dr. Myers—the department chair—about this? I already mentioned something to him in the hallway.

conversation_transcript.speaker: User B
conversation_transcript.text: Only inform him you’ve been subpoenaed as a witness, without sharing case specifics.

conversation_transcript.speaker: User A
conversation_transcript.text: Understood. What about the HR person who reached out earlier? She seemed curious.

conversation_transcript.speaker: User B
conversation_transcript.text: Direct her questions to me. You’re not obligated to provide details.

conversation_transcript.speaker: User A
conversation_transcript.text: Okay, I’ll forward anything from her to you.

conversation_transcript.speaker: User B
conversation_transcript.text: Thank you. If anyone else approaches you about it, refer them here as well.

conversation_transcript.speaker: User A
conversation_transcript.text: Will do. Are there any forms I need to sign before the deposition?

conversation_transcript.speaker: User B
conversation_transcript.text: I’ll send you a consent form and a witness information sheet by email this afternoon.

conversation_transcript.speaker: User A
conversation_transcript.text: Alright, I’ll keep an eye on it. Is there a dress code for that day?

conversation_transcript.speaker: User B
conversation_transcript.text: Business attire—something you’d wear for a meeting here or in court.

conversation_transcript.speaker: User A
conversation_transcript.text: Okay. My usual suit then. By the way, did the coordinator say how long I’ll actually be in that room?

conversation_transcript.speaker: User B
conversation_transcript.text: They estimate about 90 minutes, but sometimes it runs shorter.

conversation_transcript.speaker: User A
conversation_transcript.text: Good to know. And you’ll have a copy of that packet with the questions?

conversation_transcript.speaker: User B
conversation_transcript.text: Yes. I’ll bring copies and review them with you right before we go in.

conversation_transcript.speaker: User A
conversation_transcript.text: What do I say if they ask about things that happened after that day?

conversation_transcript.speaker: User B
conversation_transcript.text: Simply say you’re only testifying about what you directly observed on the date in question.

conversation_transcript.speaker: User A
conversation_transcript.text: Great. I’ll try to keep that clear. Is that person—the court reporter—likely to ask me anything directly?

conversation_transcript.speaker: User B
conversation_transcript.text: No, the court reporter just records. No direct questions.

conversation_transcript.speaker: User A
conversation_transcript.text: I see. And if someone interrupts us, should I just pause or can I step out?

conversation_transcript.speaker: User B
conversation_transcript.text: If a break is needed, just let me know—I'll request one.

conversation_transcript.speaker: User A
conversation_transcript.text: Alright. If my clinic tries to call me during the proceeding, is it okay to answer?

conversation_transcript.speaker: User B
conversation_transcript.text: Only if there’s a true emergency. Otherwise, silence your phone during the deposition.

conversation_transcript.speaker: User A
conversation_transcript.text: Understood. Do I have to keep my phone off, or just silent?

conversation_transcript.speaker: User B
conversation_transcript.text: Silent is fine. Just don’t check it during questioning.

conversation_transcript.speaker: User A
conversation_transcript.text: Alright, sounds doable. Is there anything else I can do to prepare?

conversation_transcript.speaker: User B
conversation_transcript.text: Keep reviewing that day’s notes and rest up. I’ll call you the evening before to check in.

conversation_transcript.speaker: User A
conversation_transcript.text: Thanks, Lara. I really appreciate your help. I feel better about handling this.

conversation_transcript.speaker: User B
conversation_transcript.text: That’s what I’m here for. We’ll get through it together.

conversation_transcript.speaker: User A
conversation_transcript.text: Okay, I’ll get ready for my next patient. Talk to you soon.

conversation_transcript.speaker: User B
conversation_transcript.text: Take care, Brian.

generation_metadata.scenario_request: Brian Foster is a 43-year-old physician practicing in San Diego, California. He has been subpoenaed as a witness in a medical malpractice lawsuit involving another doctor at his hospital. Brian, worried about professional implications and time away from his practice, consults attorney Lara Washington, who is retained to guide him through the deposition process. Lara explains the nature of a subpoena and the expectations for testimony, including the procedural requirements of the discovery process. She reviews Brian’s anticipated testimony, ensuring it remains within the limits of his direct knowledge and does not disclose privileged information. Brian is anxious about being cross-examined and about balancing professional courtesy with legal obligations. Lara coaches him on answering interrogatories and maintaining clarity and objectivity. She discusses the importance of truthfulness, the boundaries of attorney-client privilege in this context, and the protections he has as a non-party witness. Lara also ensures that Brian’s employer is informed without breaching confidentiality. As the deposition nears, Brian feels more prepared, trusting in Lara’s guidance to navigate the legal and professional challenges ahead.
